question: An ice-cream novelty item consists of a cup in the shape of a \(4\)-inch-tall frustum of a right circular cone, with a \(2\)-inch-diameter base at the bottom and a \(4\)-inch-diameter base at the top, packed solid with ice cream, together with a solid cone of ice cream of height \(4\) inches, whose base, at the bottom, is the top base of the frustum. What is the total volume of the ice cream, in cubic inches?
solution:
The frustum can be viewed as a large cone with a smaller cone removed. Its base radii are \(1\) inch and \(2\) inches.

Extend the frustum's sloping sides downward to their common apex \(P\). Let \(O\) and \(T\) be the centers of the bottom and top bases, respectively, and let \(PO=x\). Then \(PT=x+4\).

An axial cross-section gives similar right triangles for the small and large cones. Their heights have the same ratio as their radii, so
\[
\frac{x+4}{x}=\frac21.
\]
Thus \(x+4=2x\), giving \(x=4\). The removed cone has height \(4\), and the large cone has height \(8\).

Using \(V=\frac13\pi r^2h\), the frustum's volume is
\[
V_{\text{frustum}}
=\frac13\pi(2)^2(8)-\frac13\pi(1)^2(4)
=\frac{32\pi-4\pi}{3}
=\frac{28\pi}{3}.
\]
The cone of ice cream above the cup has radius \(2\) and height \(4\), so its volume is
\[
V_{\text{top}}=\frac13\pi(2)^2(4)=\frac{16\pi}{3}.
\]
Adding the two parts gives
\[
V=\frac{28\pi}{3}+\frac{16\pi}{3}
=\boxed{\frac{44\pi}{3}}\text{ cubic inches}.
\]
The answer is \(\textbf{(E)}\).
